claim: A rotary's acceleration byte is read through its top four bits, and the sixteen entries that leaves are what the rotor's loop multiplies the difference by before shifting it. So the distance the rotor stops short of the rate entry it was aimed at is one constant divided by what the entry holds. What the entries hold is a sequence: the first ten count up, one through ten, and then they double -- twelve, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, a hundred and twenty-eight. 14 of the sixteen are readable and 12 of those land on that sequence inside what their own take told a rate apart to, with one constant over the whole table and nothing else fitted. The last one does not: it reads 168 where the doubling says 256, five times what the take resolves, and it is published as the number it is. The byte is not a shift count, which is what a four-bit acceleration invited: the distance does not halve per step of it, and the near-four between the two rotors' defaults is where those two defaults happen to sit in this table. The two rotors are one routine reached twice -- at nine settings of the byte their distances agree to a median of 2.8 per cent. And the constant, 0.9768 Hz, names the clock a fifth time by a route none of the other four used: it is a rate divided by a power of two, and at thirty-two kilohertz that power is 14.9996 while at forty-four and forty-eight no integer power comes within four tenths.
named: a four-bit acceleration that multiplies the difference before the shift
adds: The records say what each rotor turned at, at each setting of the byte the page calls its acceleration, with the other rotor silenced and the rate byte held. What is read out of them here is that the byte is taken by its top four bits, that the sixteen entries are a multiplier rather than a shift count, what that multiplier is over the first ten of them, what the constant is, and that the constant is a clock over a power of two. The records name no bits, no multiplier and no clock, and say so.
refutedBy: Two settings inside one run of eight returning different distances, which would take the four bits away. Or the two rotors returning different distances at one setting of the byte, which would make them two routines and put the four to one back on the rotors. Or the constant turning out to depend on the entry the rotor was aimed at, which would make it a ratio rather than a distance -- the same entry has now been read aimed at 10.00 Hz and at 0.8488, twelve times apart, and the two distances differ by 0.0001 Hz. Or an entry of the sequence moving off its whole number as the entry it was aimed at is measured rather than fitted, which is what the standing alternative asks.

rows: Rotary, parameter 3, Low Accl (Low frequency Acceleration), 0 - 15

eraPriors.claim: A control processor of this period closes a lag with a subtract, a shift and an add, and the only cheap place to put a per-parameter amount in it is a multiply of the difference before the shift. A multiply by a small integer is a shift and an add or two; a divide is neither.
eraPriors.why: It is what makes a distance of one constant over a small integer the thing to look for rather than a distance halving per step, and the records say which of the two it is.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The multiplier had turned out to be a power of two per step, which is the reading this claim replaces.

alternatives.reading: The entry is a shift count, so the distance halves at every step of it -- which is what a four-bit acceleration invites and what the rate claim beside this one read into the four to one between the two rotors.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The shape of the table. Scored through the same gates it is 0.01475 octaves against the winner's 0.00046, and it fails where its own structure lives: a halving per step is a factor of thirty-two over the five entries between the two rotors' defaults, and the records put them a factor of four apart.

alternatives.reading: The multiplier is taken from the whole byte rather than from its top four bits.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: A property, not a residual -- on the median it is 0.00219 against 0.00046 and that is not what decides it. Four runs of eight were read at two settings each, and the distances inside them agree to between 0.02 and 0.67 per cent. A whole byte puts the same pairs between 7.9 and 700.0 per cent apart.

alternatives.reading: The byte does not set the distance at all, and the two rotors' distances differ because the rotors do.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The sweep. The distance runs from 0.9728 Hz to 0.0029 Hz across the byte, a factor of 335, and the low rotor set to the high rotor's default returns the high rotor's distance.

alternatives.reading: The multiplier above the tenth entry is a law of its own rather than four numbers -- the table's top half on a different footing from its bottom half, which is what a hand-made table looks like and also what a second formula looks like.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The run it queued, once the entry the rotor was aimed at had been measured rather than fitted. It is a law and not four numbers: above the tenth entry the table doubles -- twelve, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, a hundred and twenty-eight -- and four of those five land inside what their own take told a rate apart to. Scored against the same records with the same single constant, the sequence is worst by 0.00356 octaves on the low rotor where the line is worst by 0.10174, which is the same comparison round one made and the first time the top of the table has been in it. The sixteenth entry is not on the sequence and is published as the number it is.

alternatives.reading: The sixteenth entry is on the doubling after all, and what is read there is the rate table's own error at the entry the rotor was aimed at rather than a distance the byte set.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The entry it was aimed at was measured, not fitted. The descent and the climb are two takes of the same evening on the same held block, so the distance between them is a difference of two readings of one quantity and a reading bias cancels in it. What is left is 0.00580 Hz against the 0.00382 the doubling asks for, and against 0.00040 Hz that the take told a rate apart to.

alternatives.reading: The entries between the tenth and the sixteenth are on whole numbers other than these -- the departures being real rather than a reading.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The bar the departures are read against, which is per entry and is the record's own. A distance is a number of hertz and the takes here tell a rate apart to between two ten-thousandths and nine thousandths of one, so the question is not how many per cent an entry is off: it is whether the reading can tell it from the sequence. 12 of 14 cannot. The two that can are entries [7, 15] -- one at 1.2 times its take's own spread, which is the bar and not a margin over it, and the last entry, which is dealt with above. Two of the entries also had the number they were subtracted from measured after this was queued, and the one that moved most moved onto its whole number: the eleventh entry read 1.7 per cent off sixteen against a fitted aim and 0.1 per cent off it against one the unit stated.

and_the_two_constants.what: One constant is fitted per rotor and they come back 0.977 Hz and 0.934. The low rotor's is read against an entry the unit stated and the high rotor's is not -- nothing has been descended onto on that rotor's rate byte -- and the high rotor's distances are four times smaller, so the same table error is four times more of them. The difference between the two constants is what that costs, and it is not evidence that the rotors differ.

gates.name: gross
gates.why: median 0.00046 octaves on the low rotor against the 2.3554 octaves this byte commands, and 0.00069 against 0.0319 on the high rotor, with one constant fitted per rotor and the two constants coming out at 0.98 and 0.999 Hz.

gates.name: properties
gates.why: Two properties, and neither is a residual. Settings that share an entry return one distance, to within a per cent on four runs of eight. And the two rotors return the same table: at nine settings of the byte their distances agree to a median of 2.8 per cent, which is what says the four to one between their defaults is the two defaults.

gates.name: power
gates.why: The shift count is beaten on the residual by a factor of 32 and the whole byte is beaten by a property it contradicts rather than by its residual, which is the stronger of the two. The byte doing nothing is in the ranking because both records that closed the rate claim had to assume it.

gates.name: breakdown
gates.why: The winner's worst is 0.03882 octaves at setting 104, against 0.00013 of floor -- which is a lean and is reported rather than explained away.

figures.read_as: It is the top of the byte and it is one-sided. From entry 10 up the multiplier runs above the line at every entry and by more at each, so the model reads the rotor as further from its target than it was. That is the alternative left standing and it carries the run that would settle it. Below that entry the residual is inside what the run resolves at every admitted setting of both rotors.

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// roland-sc8850-01  ·  01 22  ·  rotor-acceleration
//
// Generated by yarn sync from inferences/models/0122-accl-a-line-then-a-doubling.json.
// The claim it closes: inferences/roland-sc8850-01/0122-an-acceleration-byte-is-four-bits-and-a-multiplier.json
//
// Every constant, every section count and every structural choice below is
// the model's. The difference equations are the ordinary realisations of the
// sections the model names — this site's arithmetic, not a measurement.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

#include <cstring>

namespace soundings::roland_sc8850_01::type_01_22 {

// The entry counts up over the first ten and then doubles: one, two, three and so on to
// ten, then twelve, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, a hundred and twenty-eight, two
// hundred and fifty-six. One constant over the whole table and a sequence with nothing
// fitted in it.

// printed range: 0.05 - 10.0
// 8 settings read, interpolated linearly between them and flat outside them
inline double at005100(int byte) {
  static const int kAt[] = {24, 32, 48, 64, 80, 88, 96, 127};
  static const double kRead[] = {9.7665, 9.8132, 9.86657142857, 9.89622222222, 9.92216666667, 9.941625, 9.9708125, 9.9963515625};
  constexpr int kCount = sizeof(kAt) / sizeof(kAt[0]);
  if (byte <= kAt[0]) return kRead[0];
  if (byte >= kAt[kCount - 1]) return kRead[kCount - 1];
  int i = 1;
  while (kAt[i] < byte) ++i;
  const double t = static_cast<double>(byte - kAt[i - 1]) / (kAt[i] - kAt[i - 1]);
  return kRead[i - 1] + t * (kRead[i] - kRead[i - 1]);
}

/**
 * Which table applies is decided by the range the page prints against the
 * address, which is a fact about the document rather than about the byte.
 */
inline bool lookUp(const char* printedRange, int byte, double& out) {
  if (std::strcmp(printedRange, "0.05 - 10.0") == 0) { out = at005100(byte); return true; }
  // A range no reading has been taken over. Saying nothing is the answer:
  // returning a neighbouring table would be inventing a measurement.
  return false;
}

}  // namespace soundings::roland_sc8850_01::type_01_22
